segments.speaker: Jekaterina Novikova
segments.text: Hello and welcome to another episode of the Women in AI Research Podcast. I'm your host, Jekaterina and I'm joined by my co-host, Malikeh. We are excited to explore the fascinating intersection of artificial intelligence, healthcare, and the AI ethics with our special guest today. And I'm excited to welcome Dr. Faiza Khan Khattak, the Chief Technology Officer of Monark Health, an innovative startup that is leveraging AI to support individuals overcoming alcohol use disorder. And other than being the entrepreneur and the CTO, Faiza is also the research scientist. And she, as a researcher, Faiza specializes in fairness in language models, diverse NLP applications, and the applied research that ensures that AI technologies are equitable and inclusive. So Faiza, it's such a pleasure to have you with us today. And to start with, could you tell us a little bit about your journey into the world of artificial intelligence?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: Thank you so much. Thanks for having me. It's so exciting to be here and be part of this Women in AI Research podcast. It was really exciting. And yes, thanks for the lovely introduction, by the way. Yeah, so I'm excited to share my AI journey, which has been very long, seems like centuries ago when I started. So yeah, I will start from the very beginning. I was...

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: My initial background is in Mathematics back home, which is Pakistan. I'm from Pakistan. So I was studying Mathematics and I taught Mathematics for a bit. And at that time, I thought that probably I want to dive deeper into the applications of mathematics, especially I wanted to go abroad to US to study and do PhD. So that's why that's how I opted for computer science. I thought that was something that was booming and that was, had more, I could have applications of mathematics and see more applied mathematics work there. So that's how I ended up at Columbia University, where I did my Master's and PhD in computer science. So since my background was in mathematics, I started with Master's in the foundation track, which is theoretical computer science. So I took a lot of theoretical courses.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: For example, like I took computational complexity, approximation algorithms, which is the advanced algorithms course, numerical algorithm complexity, graph theory, and other courses like quantum computing and the regular AI courses like AI and machine learning and advanced machine learning, all these courses. So I had that background in mathematics and theory, theoretical computer science. So I decided when I was choosing my advisor for PhD, ended up, I got interested in machine learning because it was something that aligned with my expertise. It involved a lot of mathematics, a lot of algorithms. So that's how I ended up in PhD in machine learning. And then I started, it really changed my perspective of things. And then I was fortunate enough as a PhD student, I did my internship at LinkedIn.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: So at that time, that was the time when I realized maybe one day I want to have my own company. So I was data scientist and intern and I was really enjoying that time. After completing my PhD, it's a long journey by the way, after completing my PhD, I came to Toronto and I got a postdoc position at University Health Network, St. Michael's Hospital. And along with that, I was affiliated to UofT (University of Toronto) and Vector Institute at the time. I did a lot of research around NLP applied to healthcare data. So that was pre-BERT era, BERT had just was coming in at that time. So I had a lot of exposure to the research in healthcare. And at the same time, I happened to teach, I got the sessional lecturer position for a semester at University of Toronto, so that's I was also teaching.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: One of my research projects and my postdoc was formed into a startup. So I got involved into that startup. So I was one of the founding members. So was really lucky to be in that time, in that place at that time. So that was really a nice experience. But afterwards, after two years, I thought that maybe I want to change the course a little bit. So I joined the industry. I joined Manulife as a data scientist. So that was a very different experience, a lot of learning there, how those companies work. And again, I was in a part of the NLP team. So for two years, I worked for Manulife. I enjoyed the work very much. But then I got an opportunity at Vector Institute as an applied machine learning scientist for NLP.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: So this experience was a of a combination of previous many experiences because I was working with the faculty members doing applied research transitioning that research and knowledge to the industry either through boot camps, helping out with camps, had applied research projects that published many papers together along with the industry and faculty. I'm the CTO and the co-founder of the startup called Monark Health. It is a spin out from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH). So we are working on building an AI therapist for an alcohol use disorder patients. And we already have a lot of interest, although we are still at a very early stage. And we hope to have the pilot study done by the end of this year. But it's a very interesting experience and the amount of interest that we got from the people who are asking about venus, this product coming, is very interesting. So that was a long, long journey.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: But I'm glad that I was one of the lucky person who could experience all different aspects of possibilities of this AI realm.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: It basically happened because I wanted to have an experience of all these and see like all these have the understanding of all these perspectives. segments.text: It's always good to reach out to people, either it's LinkedIn or like at a conference and ask for mentorship or ask for guidance. segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: There is a lot of support if you want to really excel.

segments.text: Yeah, that's great. I think something that you raised about mentorship, that's really one of my dream goals. segments.speaker: Jekaterina Novikova
segments.text: I agree completely. Also one aspect that I wanted to dive deeper into is, Faiza, you have mentioned that it is more difficult for women to thrive in many fields and in the field of research and AI probably in particular. So people trusted me, people gave me the opportunities. That's why I am who I am today. It would have been very hard for me to be able to do the work that I have done. But at the same time, yes, directly or indirectly, I have at times seen unconscious bias towards women. And I'm not blaming anyone because this unconscious bias, people are not sometimes aware of that when they ask something from a female colleague or a female maybe like the manager and then they want to confirm it from a male colleague of them. So just to see, it's not that they're doing it intentionally, but somehow something subconsciously implies somewhere that maybe they know better.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: One of the things is that, and I think so it's reducing with the passage of time as more and women are being involved in this field. And the other type of things that people have told me is that sometimes people are intimidated by a female who has better profile than them and has done better, that better work than them, which is again, very subtle, which I feel bad because men are raised in such a way that they are, they are always told to be the stronger person and it's not their fault. It's not anybody's fault, but it's just like sometimes you have to change the perspective. So this is something that needs to be changed, I think. And it is, it has changed over the past many years. But unfortunately, unfortunately there are subtle biases still existing.

segments.speaker: Jekaterina Novikova
segments.text: I like how you put it into the perspective that it's not to blame people. And I completely agree. It's not about the blame. Especially given that it's not when it comes to the women focus biased, it's not even only it's not only coming from men, right? We have those biases ourselves as well. Yeah, or do you have maybe some additional advice on what to do with that?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: So for women, I always tell them don't be intimidated. Because women have this thing called imposter syndrome more often than men. And we underestimate ourselves a lot. We like tend to, women don't, it's a research that women don't apply to most of the jobs unless they're.. because they don't feel qualified enough, even if they have like 90 % of the credentials and men apply even if they have like 70 % for most. I'm not trying to be biased here, but it's the way that women usually think. So don't be intimidated. Don't consider yourself a woman, just consider yourself. And if you're an AI researcher, an AI expert, or a student, whatever you are, just consider yourself that and just apply for all the opportunities and get help. Whenever you don't understand anything, there are many people, plenty of people who are there to help you. And many people reach out to me as well. So I try to do as much as I can.

segments.speaker: Malikeh Ehghaghi
segments.text: Yeah, I cannot agree more. Thank you. Amazing. Now, let's shift our focus to your research a bit. In one of your papers, which is called MLHOps: Machine Learning for Health Operations, you introduced a pipeline for reliable, efficient, and ethical deployment of ML models on healthcare settings, which is a fantastic paper, and I'm really glad that some people worked on that.

segments.speaker: Malikeh Ehghaghi
segments.text: Can you tell us about this work and why it is important, especially in healthcare domain?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: So, AI adoption is becoming more important and because every most of the institutes want to like incorporate AI into their work. And especially in healthcare, AI is really important because of multiple reasons because AI is that's something that can help the clinicians in our like healthcare providers to provide better healthcare and as well at the same time being more cost effective. Now in this paper we have discussed the MLOps pipeline for healthcare which is called MLOps, ML Machine Learning Healthcare Operations, So what we have focused on this, this paper is basically providing the survey of all the best practices and all the important aspects of a health MLOps pipeline in particular for healthcare.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: So basically, it's a combination of how to deal with data, how to store that, how to deal with machine learning models, how to deploy those models, and how to keep track of them, keep track of the data shift, or any sort of changes, continuous monitoring and continuous development, that type of work. And it also has, since MLOps is quite broad, it also discusses the responsible AI aspect of that. So it extends the traditional MLops principles to healthcare by integrating not just the technical aspects, but also how they can be, the whole pipeline can be made more explainable, more fair and interpretable. So this is a whole recipe for clinicians or healthcare providers who want to incorporate machine learning in their system. Also, we have provided a checklist at the end of the paper that helps different people to understand what are the important aspects at each stage and what are the measures that they need to take at different

segments.speaker: Jekaterina Novikova
segments.text: Right, it sounds like a very important work. Can you please explain for people who are more ML oriented rather than healthcare oriented, how is the operationalization of ML models in healthcare domains specifically, how is it different from other application domains?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: So first of all, while a lot of things remain the same, still the model has to work better and all that, this is the most high stakes application of AI because of a small mistake, a misdiagnosis or something that wrong recommendation can lead to really serious consequences. So we always want to avoid that. So the main important thing is that like Making an error is not just like recommending a wrong movie. It's like some can cause somebody life or even like or life or something else like it can have serious consequences. So that's the most important thing. And That's why the greater care has to be taken in this deployment of ML systems in the healthcare settings. segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: So at the same time, fairness is another aspect. And we have seen a lot of research where has seen that different models, even in healthcare settings, have very biased like outputs in some cases, or biased results. So that is another important thing that we want to know that how different populations are treated by a model, an AI model that is being used in the healthcare. And other than that, there are of course, regulatory compliance and continuous improvement, there could be change in data, like in the times of COVID, we had seen a lot of things have changed. So that was a drastic change in healthcare data. So there could be many different things was overall, I would say that it's it's involved more risk and more AI and safety has to be involved there.

segments.speaker: Jekaterina Novikova
segments.text: I have a very similar experience from my own previous research experience in ML models in clinical settings, especially with trust. think trust, transparency and interpretability is something that is not just a research question. It's something that could be the highest blocker when it comes to the adoption of the technology.

segments.speaker: Malikeh Ehghaghi
segments.text: So in particular, how does MLHOps help approach explainability and transparency in AI models?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: Yeah, so these MLHOps whole pipeline is something that has been well thought in advance. It's not that you build a model and later you think about like having, maybe we should be interpretable enough. One of the things that we recommend in this paper is that, there should be different levels of explainability and transparency because there might be some explanation which is good and not good for a clinician who is able to understand many aspects, right? segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: It can help with privacy and security as well. Bias detection is one of the things and that we have in our work, have also used interpretability and expeditability to detect the bias because once we know how the model is working, how the thought process of the model is going on, that is something that helps us to understand if the model is biased.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: At the same time, there are other aspects of explainability that need to be like, that need more attention. How are we going to evaluate that?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: And one more thing that since even for like when we have these language models or ChatGPT we have been relying more on AI instead of using our own like understanding or expertise. segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: At the same time, since AI models and we know that have been prone to bias, and there are a lot of things that can impact the decision of the model in terms of being unfair or biased, which could come through different sources. It could be, bias could come from the AI model itself, the way it's working. segments.speaker: Malikeh Ehghaghi
segments.text: Amazing, thank you. You've also done some truly compelling work addressing social bias in particular within AI systems. In one of your paper, that is called, Using Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Interpretable Recognition of Social Bias, you speak about how to address biases in language models and in particular, you demonstrate the importance of reasoning in zero-shot stereotype identification.

segments.speaker: Malikeh Ehghaghi
segments.text: Can you tell us more about this research and its findings?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: Yeah, so that paper actually basically is a very nice example of combining interpretability and explainability for detecting bias. But in this particular paper, we focused on social bias, which is it's very subtle and sometimes you don't even realize, even in human beings, we don't realize that there's some sort of social bias and we are just assuming things. So this was the paper where we discussed that if we try to like ask the model to reason before it gives us an answer, the model is better able to understand what is happening.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: Or it may be able to identify its bias and realize it before answering the question that we got better results even with the relatively smaller models. Here I want to mention one of the more recent research that we have done and recently the paper was published at AAAI Symposium, Spring Symposium, which was very interesting. It was a preliminary work and it was done along with my colleagues at the University. So that was that dialectical bias that like language models behave differently for African American English versus standard American English. So that was an interesting study that we did. segments.speaker: Jekaterina Novikova

segments.text: I, because I completely agree, it's a very subtle, subtle concept. On the one hand, on the other hand, it's a sufficiently broad one. So you mentioned that dialectical bias, which is also under the umbrella of social bias, right? So how do we define the concept of social bias?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: Yeah, social bias can be very broad and very subtle. Most of it, I mean, a lot of it could be conscious bias, but a lot of it is unintentional. We don't even know. We just like stereotype people. Certain type of people do this, and certain type of people do this, and this ethnicity behaves like this. So that's a very subtle type of bias, but it's more generally defined as having discriminatory behavior towards them. It could be an individual or group usually, or like specific nationalities or ethnic groups or beliefs, and which results into like, results into a prejudiced or unfair behavior. So that's how it defines social bias. And that can, it can be manifested in different ways, as I said, that it could be either like associating a certain sort of associate like work or attribute towards women. For example, most of the people say women are bad drivers, right? So that's something that is assumed and sometimes, yeah, it's more like intentional in this case, but at the same time as we say that if somebody is speaking, it has an accent like a non-native speaker like me. So that also causes some sort of bias once you call someone and they say, yeah, non-native speaker, so they bite me.

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: Not saying that. Yeah, so language models are prone to that as well.

segments.speaker: Jekaterina Novikova
segments.text: Mm.

segments.speaker: Malikeh Ehghaghi
segments.text: Interesting. Again, going back to that paper that I mentioned, that chain-of-thought prompting thing, you in particular demonstrate the importance of reasoning. So I'm curious, what is the relationship between reasoning and interpretability in this setting?

segments.speaker: Faiza Khan Khattak
segments.text: So it's like asking someone to answer a question, not just saying yes and no, rather first thinking out loud and describing the different thought processes. So while describing that, of the benefits that we get is that the model, we are able to understand that how the problem is being solved or how in this case social bias is being evaluated. So it helps us in understanding the model's thought process and see what deficiencies or what wrong beliefs it is using to come to that conclusion. But at the same time, while it helps us understand how the model is processing the question, it also helps us in understanding the core concept and it also helps the model itself to understand and realize the mistakes. And we have seen that if it just directly blurs the answer yes or no, the performance is lower as compared to when we ask it to break down the problem and think and then its answer is better or like it has a better like a better accuracy. And In some cases the models try to stick to wrong answers if the reasoning happens afterwards. They try to come up with the reasoning to support their wrong answer. But so if you ask the model to give the reasoning first, it realizes just like normal human beings, it has ego issues probably. So if it starts with the reasoning, it is able to come to the right answer. But if it gives the wrong answer first, it ends up making up stuff to support its answer. It doesn't want to look bad in front of people.
